goal: A browser game of Tetris that a person can actually sit down and play. Pieces fall and can be moved, rotated and dropped; filled lines clear and score; the game speeds up and eventually ends. It should be clear at a glance what is happening and what is coming next. It runs by opening one HTML file, is controlled from the keyboard, and feels responsive rather than sluggish.

No page errors in either across ~15 test sequences. B pulls ahead on completeness/polish of the same correct mechanics: its terminal state and score are real DOM text (confirmed literally reading 'GAME OVER 228 Tap to return to menu' in the page's own text after topping out), and its difficulty ramp (speed + lock delay + DAS) scales together across a real level ladder, whereas A is functionally solid but its end-state is pixels-only and its progression is a single coarse threshold.

Fix: toggle a DOM element (e.g. a hidden <div id="gameover"> shown when `over` becomes true) in A instead of relying solely on canvas text, so the terminal state is legible without reading pixels.

history.why: Both engines pass the baseline mechanics under direct testing with node scripts/play.mjs: lateral movement to both walls, rotation with wall-kick tables (verified S/Z pieces kicking cleanly off both walls in repeated trials, no clipping, no page errors under 120-key randomized mashing), soft drop, hard drop, board accumulation, and a Game Over state on top-out (confirmed explicitly for both: A shows canvas text "Game Over" after ~24 stacked hard-drops; B shows a "GAME OVER <score> Tap to return to menu" overlay after 22 stacked hard-drops). Where they diverge, on things actually run rather than read: (1) Score feedback. A's score only increments on a completed line clear (score += table[cleared] in lockPiece()); across every session I actually drove against A — plain movement+drop, a deliberate column-by-column sweep meant to line up a full row, and 120-key randomized mashing — the on-screen "Score 0" text never moved once, because no row was ever completed before the pile topped out. B's score visibly and reliably moved in every equivalent run (38 -> 72 -> 96 -> 188 -> 200 -> 210 -> 308) because it also awards points for hard-drop distance, so the one HUD element that tells a player "my input is doing something" is live from the first drop. (2) Gravity/robustness. A's fall tick is a single `if (t - last > dropMs) piece.y++` per frame with no delta accumulation, so it has no protection against multi-frame teleporting or, conversely, stalling under a hitch; B accumulates a delta-time dropTimer, clamps it against post-hitch catch-up, and steps gravity in a while-loop, which is the more defensible implementation for staying responsive under variable frame timing (the goal's explicit "feels responsive rather than sluggish"). (3) Once Game Over, A has no restart path at all (`if (over) return` swallows every key), so a finished session is a dead end requiring a page reload; B lets a keypress restart from the game-over screen. Both implement the speed-up mechanism identically in spirit (level derived from lines cleared, not raw elapsed time), so neither wins on that specific claim in this testing.
history.gap: A's score is wired exclusively to full-row completion with zero credit for hard/soft drop distance, and combined with its plain (non-bagged) RNG and staircase-prone stacking, this means the single visible feedback signal a player has (the score text) stayed at literal "0" through every scripted session I ran against it, including sequences built specifically to fill a row and sequences of 100+ mixed inputs — the number the goal asks to "read as non-zero/increasing" simply doesn't move in ordinary early play. Wiring at least the hard/soft drop distance into score (as B does) would make the HUD demonstrate live responsiveness immediately instead of only after a player manages a full clear.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 3: A's game-over transition is not a latched terminal state: in doc-2.html's keydown handler, `if (gameOver) { ... else { gameoverOverlay.classList.add("hidden"); startGame(); } }` means any key other than Escape immediately restarts the game (score→0, board cleared) instead of staying on the Game Over screen. B guards its entire keydown handler with `if (over) return`, so once over, it stays over. Fix for A: while gameOver is true, ignore ordinary gameplay keys (Space/arrows/etc.) and require a distinct, deliberate action (e.g. only Enter, or clicking a 'play again' button) to restart.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 4: Artifact A has no way to restart or replay after Game Over: the keydown listener short-circuits on `over` with no code path anywhere in the file that ever sets `over = false` again, so once the game ends the only way to play again is to manually reload the HTML file outside the game entirely. B implements a full restart flow (any key after Game Over, or the Restart button, calls startGame() which resets gameOver, score, board and level). Given the stated goal explicitly includes a game that 'eventually ends' and is 'controlled from the keyboard,' a Tetris implementation a person can 'actually sit down and play' needs to be replayable from the keyboard without touching the browser/file — this is a complete, verified-live functional absence in A, not a matter of degree.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 5: doc-1.html's (B's) piece spawner (`function spawn(){ const i = Math.floor(Math.random()*SHAPES.length); ... }`) draws each new piece independently and uniformly at random with no history/bag mechanism, so it can produce unbounded streaks or droughts of any single piece type across a session. doc-2.html (A) replaces this with a Fisher–Yates-shuffled 7-bag (`shuffledBag()` + `nextPiece()`) that guarantees each of the 7 piece types is dealt exactly once per 7 spawns. To close the gap, B needs the same bag-based generator swapped in for its naive per-spawn RNG call — everything else in B's core mechanics (movement, SRS kicks, lock delay, hard/soft drop scoring, line-clear-and-collapse, Game Over/restart, speed curve) already tested correct and on par with A.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 6: A's difficulty ramp exists in code (dropMs shrinks with score) but is not reachable or observable through the intended play pattern: the game reliably ends (score in the low hundreds) before the 500-point threshold for the first speed tier is crossed, and every further keypress after Game Over — not just Space — immediately calls startGame() and resets score to 0 with no confirmation or persistent end screen, so a player (or this test) can never accumulate enough score across a single life to see or feel the game get faster. Fix: either lower the score-per-tier threshold drastically (or key speed-up to something reachable via hard-drop distance alone, like distance-dropped or piece count) so a single, realistic play session actually demonstrates acceleration, and/or stop treating every key as an implicit restart once over is true so a tester/player can at least see the final board and score before it vanishes.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 7: A's fall-speed ramp is gated exclusively on lines cleared (`level = Math.floor(lines/10)+1` feeding `getSpeed(level)`), so a session that stacks pieces without completing a row never gets any faster — confirmed live (level/lines panels frozen at 1/0 across 40 additional hard drops in one column, score only rising by the flat hard-drop bonus). It needs a speed input that also advances with pieces placed or elapsed time, not lines alone, so the game visibly speeds up even for a player who is stacking badly and never clearing a row — the exact case the goal's "the game speeds up ... and eventually ends" is describing.

core-gameplay-mechanics round 8: B's soft-drop control is a held-key state (`keys["down"]`) polled once per animation frame with a 50ms accumulation threshold before it moves the piece, rather than a discrete step-on-keypress. Under the prescribed test methodology (and under any quick tap of the key) this yields a literal zero: no downward movement, no score change, verified by an identical screenshot and identical score (38) between an ArrowDown-only run and an ArrowLeft/ArrowRight control run of the same length. Fix: make ArrowDown also perform one immediate discrete downward step (and its associated point) on keydown, independent of how long the key is subsequently held, the way A's `down()` does.

at-a-glance-clarity round 1: Artifact B has no next-piece preview at all — a player looking at the static frame cannot see what piece is coming next to plan rotation/placement before it lands, which is the specific capability this part of the judgment is checking for.

at-a-glance-clarity round 2: A's board has no grid at all — the entire play field is a flat, undifferentiated black rectangle with only an outer border, so a player cannot judge column alignment or row position at a glance; B renders a full grid across every cell of the board.

at-a-glance-clarity round 3: B has no visual hierarchy separating primary game state (board, score, next-piece) from secondary text (control instructions, game-over banner) — both render at comparable size/weight and screen area, so the eye must search past a wall of text to find the game state instead of landing on it immediately.

at-a-glance-clarity round 4: A's Score/Next are not grouped into a unified, bordered/labeled HUD panel the way B's Next/Hold/Score/Menu strip is, and the glanceable viewport is diluted by a block of plain instructional prose occupying the space where a player's eye would otherwise scan for live state — group/label the HUD elements and remove the instructions text from the primary at-a-glance view.

at-a-glance-clarity round 5: B's dark locked-piece color (~RGB 52,12,85) sits too close in luminance to its dark navy board background (~RGB 17,17,34); it needs to be lightened/desaturated-up (or given a visible stroke/outline) so that every piece color, not just the brighter ones, stays visually distinct from the empty board at a glance.

at-a-glance-clarity round 6: B's locked-piece fill color for at least one piece type (dark purple, RGB 52,12,85) has a contrast ratio of only ~1.18:1 against the board background (17,17,34) — essentially the same luminance — so that portion of the locked stack is nearly invisible against the board rather than clearly outlined; A keeps every piece color it renders above 10:1 contrast against its pure-black board. Fix: raise the minimum luminance/saturation floor for locked-block fills (or add a stroke/outline per cell) so no piece color drops below roughly a 3:1 contrast ratio against the board fill, regardless of which piece type locked there.

at-a-glance-clarity round 7: B has no ghost/landing-preview piece: locked and falling blocks are drawn with the same full-opacity fill (confirmed by pixel sampling: locked cyan (0,255,255) is exactly as saturated as it would be while falling), so distinguishing "in motion" from "already placed" relies purely on incidental hue differences between piece types rather than any systematic visual encoding, and nothing in the static frame shows where the current piece will land — add a muted/outlined silhouette of the current piece at its drop position, as A does.

at-a-glance-clarity round 8: B's ghost/landing-preview piece is rendered as a solid, low-opacity fill in the same color family as the falling piece and the real locked stack, so it is distinguished from an actually-placed block only by a brightness/saturation difference rather than by a clean fill-vs-outline distinction — at a glance it risks reading as an already-locked piece rather than a preview. A avoids this by rendering its ghost with zero interior fill (matching the empty-cell background exactly) and only a colored border, making falling piece, landing preview, and locked terrain three unmistakably different visual states.

at-a-glance-clarity round 9: Give the play field its own explicit border/frame drawn directly against the board background (not just relying on the difference between two very similar dark tones), and remove or repurpose the empty margin currently sitting beside the grid — right now the board's true edge in A is discoverable only by tracing where the internal grid lines stop, not by any deliberate boundary.

Each built round asks one fresh critic which is closer to the goal — the version this round produced, or the copy taken before it — and the answer is recorded per round as `regression`, with `regressed: true` on any round the critic judged worse than what it replaced. A wrong revert is also quieter than a wrong refusal, which at least stops the run loudly. Nothing in this plugin checks that a critic could have failed — no defect is planted, no control is run on a clean copy, and a critic that approves everything is indistinguishable from a critic that is right. The seeded-defect machinery that used to do this lived in the review panel and was deleted with it; this is now the plugin's largest unmeasured property, not a lane that exists elsewhere.

The breaker is checked at ROUND BOUNDARIES, not continuously. Removing the token while a critic or builder is mid-flight does not abort that agent — the run stops before the next round starts. To stop a round already in progress, kill the workflow itself.
Nothing stops the token being re-created after a cancel. The breaker reports the state at each boundary; it does not latch.

With no budget target set, there is no pre-committed ceiling at all — the run continues until it wins, an agent fails, or the operator cancels. That is the source design rather than an oversight — it says "there should be no arbitrary final round" — and it means an unattended run is bounded only by the host's own runaway backstop.
